dampfnudel.name: Dampfnudel
dampfnudel.summary: A steamed dumpling eaten as a meal or dessert in southern Germany, Austria, Switzerland and Alsace, and a typical southern German dish.

house-of-wittelsbach.name: Wittelsbach family
house-of-wittelsbach.summary: A Bavarian dynasty that ruled territories including Bavaria, the Palatinate and, at times, Sweden, Denmark and Hungary, with three members becoming Holy Roman Emperor.

wei-wurst.name: Weißwurst
wei-wurst.summary: Traditional Bavarian sausage of minced veal and pork fatback, historically made fresh each morning and, by custom, never eaten after midday.

kn-del.name: Knödel
kn-del.summary: Boiled dumplings found across Central and Eastern European cuisine, usually made from flour, bread or potatoes, served as a side dish or sometimes dessert.

karl-friedrich-schinkel.name: Karl Friedrich Schinkel
karl-friedrich-schinkel.summary: Prussian architect, city planner and painter (1781-1841), one of the greatest German architects and a leader of the Neoclassical and Gothic Revival movements, whose most famous buildings shaped Berlin.

aeg-turbine-factory.name: AEG Turbine Hall
aeg-turbine-factory.summary: A steel-framed factory building completed in Berlin in 1909, designed by Peter Behrens and considered the first attempt to bring modern design into industrial architecture.

peter-behrens.name: Peter Behrens
peter-behrens.summary: German architect and designer (1868–1940) known for Berlin's AEG Turbine Hall (1909), who mentored Mies van der Rohe, Le Corbusier and Walter Gropius.

fagus-factory.name: Fagus Factory
fagus-factory.summary: A shoe-last factory in Alfeld, Germany, designed by Walter Gropius and built in 1911-1913, regarded as an early landmark of modern architecture and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

walter-gropius.name: Walter Gropius
walter-gropius.summary: A German-American architect (1883–1969) who founded the Bauhaus school in Weimar in 1919 and became a leading figure of modernist, international-style architecture.

alfeld.name: Alfeld
alfeld.summary: A town in Lower Saxony, Germany, on the Leine river near Hildesheim, made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011 for its Fagus Factory.

die-br-cke.name: Die Brücke
die-br-cke.summary: German expressionist artists' group formed in Dresden in 1905 by Fritz Bleyl, Erich Heckel, Ernst Ludwig Kirchner and Karl Schmidt-Rottluff, influential in the birth of modern expressionism before dissolving around 1913.

fritz-bleyl.name: Fritz Bleyl
fritz-bleyl.summary: German Expressionist artist (1880-1966) and one of the four founders of the artist group Die Brücke, who left after two years to support his family.

erich-heckel.name: Erich Heckel
erich-heckel.summary: German painter and printmaker (1883–1970), a founding member of the group Die Brücke, which existed from 1905 to 1913.

ernst-ludwig-kirchner.name: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner
ernst-ludwig-kirchner.summary: German expressionist painter and printmaker (1880–1938), a founder of the Die Brücke art group; the Nazis later destroyed or sold over 600 of his works as "degenerate."

karl-schmidt-rottluff.name: Karl Schmidt-Rottluff
karl-schmidt-rottluff.summary: German expressionist painter and printmaker (1884-1976), one of the four founders of the artist group Die Brücke.

neue-wache.name: Neue Wache
neue-wache.summary: A guardhouse built in Berlin from 1816 to 1818 by Karl Friedrich Schinkel, later turned into Germany's Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and a national memorial to victims of war and tyranny.

altes-museum.name: Altes Museum
altes-museum.summary: Neoclassical museum building on Berlin's Museum Island, built between 1825 and 1830 by Karl Friedrich Schinkel for King Frederick William III of Prussia.

museum-island.name: Museum Island
museum-island.summary: Museum complex on an island in the Spree River in central Berlin, built from 1830 to 1930 and named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999.

gottfried-semper.name: Gottfried Semper
gottfried-semper.summary: A German architect (1803–1879) who designed Dresden's Semper Opera House and wrote influential works on the origins of architecture, after fleeing Germany for his role in the 1849 Dresden uprising.

zwinger-dresden.name: Zwinger
zwinger-dresden.summary: A palatial complex with gardens in Dresden, Germany, designed by Matthäus Daniel Pöppelmann and built in 1709 as one of Germany's most important Baroque buildings.

semperoper.name: Semperoper
semperoper.summary: The opera house of the Saxon State Opera in Dresden, Germany, built in 1841 by architect Gottfried Semper, rebuilt after an 1869 fire and completed in 1878.

schwerin-castle.name: Schwerin Palace
schwerin-castle.summary: 19th-century historicist palace on an island in Schwerin, Germany, built 1845-1857 by leading architects including Gottfried Semper; long a ducal residence, now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

der-blaue-reiter.name: Der Blaue Reiter
der-blaue-reiter.summary: A loose network of early 20th-century artists in Munich, led by Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc, whose exhibitions and almanac made them pioneers of German Expressionism before disbanding in 1914.

wassily-kandinsky.name: Wassily Kandinsky
wassily-kandinsky.summary: A Russian painter and art theorist (1866–1944) regarded as a pioneer of abstract art, who taught at the Bauhaus before settling in France.

franz-marc.name: Franz Marc
franz-marc.summary: German painter (1880–1916), a founding member of the Der Blaue Reiter group and key figure of German Expressionism known for brightly colored animal paintings; died in World War I.

august-macke.name: August Macke
august-macke.summary: German Expressionist painter (1887–1914) and a leading member of the Der Blaue Reiter group, killed in the First World War.

neue-k-nstlervereinigung-m-nchen.name: Neue Künstlervereinigung München
neue-k-nstlervereinigung-m-nchen.summary: An Expressionist artists' group founded in Munich in 1909, which prefigured Der Blaue Reiter and is seen as a forerunner of 20th-century German modern art.

wilhelm-ii.name: Wilhelm II
wilhelm-ii.summary: The last German Emperor, reigning from 1888 until his abdication in 1918, whose provocative policies helped alienate Germany from much of Europe.

k-the-kollwitz.name: Käthe Kollwitz
k-the-kollwitz.summary: German artist (1867–1945) working in painting, printmaking and sculpture, best known for art cycles depicting poverty, hunger and war on the working class; first woman elected to the Prussian Academy of Arts.

gro-e-berliner-kunstausstellung.name: Große Berliner Kunstausstellung
gro-e-berliner-kunstausstellung.summary: An annual art exhibition held in Berlin from 1893 to 1969, with a break during World War I when it moved to Düsseldorf.

konzerthaus-berlin.name: Schinkel's Schauspielhaus
konzerthaus-berlin.summary: Theatre building on Berlin's Gendarmenmarkt, operating from 1818 to 1821 as the Schauspielhaus Berlin; it became a concert hall after World War II and was renamed Konzerthaus Berlin in 1994.

gendarmenmarkt.name: Gendarmenmarkt
gendarmenmarkt.summary: A square in Berlin, created in the late 17th century, home to a concert hall and two churches and named after a Prussian cavalry regiment once stationed there.

corinthian-order.name: Corinthian order
corinthian-order.summary: The last and most ornate of the three classical orders of ancient Greek and Roman architecture, identified by column capitals carved with acanthus leaves.

historicism-art.name: Historicism
historicism-art.summary: Artistic styles, especially in 19th-century architecture, that draw inspiration from recreating or imitating earlier historic styles.

max-nordau.name: Max Nordau
max-nordau.summary: Jewish Zionist leader, physician and social critic (1849–1923) who co-founded the Zionist Organization with Theodor Herzl and became a leading early critic of modernism.

degeneration-nordau.name: Degeneration
degeneration-nordau.summary: An 1892-1893 two-volume work by Max Nordau attacking modern art as a symptom of mental and social decline, treating unconventional artists as sick and in need of therapy.

cesare-lombroso.name: Cesare Lombroso
cesare-lombroso.summary: An Italian physician (1835-1909) considered the founder of modern criminology, who argued criminality was inherited and that 'born criminals' could be identified by physical defects.

napoleon.name: Napoleon
napoleon.summary: French emperor from 1804 to 1814, and briefly in 1815, who rose to power as a general during the French Revolution and led sweeping military campaigns across Europe and the Middle East.

francis-ii-holy-roman-emperor.name: Francis II, Holy Roman Emperor
francis-ii-holy-roman-emperor.summary: Last Holy Roman Emperor, reigning until 1806, and first Emperor of Austria from 1804 as Francis I; he abdicated as Holy Roman Emperor after Napoleon founded the Confederation of the Rhine, ending that empire.

house-of-habsburg.name: Habsburg dynasty
house-of-habsburg.summary: One of Europe's most powerful dynasties, ruling the Holy Roman Empire, Austria and Spain from the Middle Ages until its male line ended in 1740.

austro-prussian-war.name: Austro-Prussian War
austro-prussian-war.summary: An 1866 war between the Austrian Empire and the Kingdom of Prussia that confirmed Prussian military superiority, shifted power among German states toward Prussia, and led to Italy gaining Venetia.

war-of-the-sixth-coalition.name: War of the Sixth Coalition
war-of-the-sixth-coalition.summary: An 1812–1814 war in which a coalition including Austria, Prussia, Russia and Britain defeated Napoleon's France and forced him into exile on Elba, following the disastrous invasion of Russia.

congress-of-vienna.name: Congress of Vienna
congress-of-vienna.summary: A series of diplomatic meetings from 1814 to 1815 that redrew Europe's political order after the downfall of Napoleon, chaired by Austrian statesman Metternich.

schleswig-holstein.name: Schleswig-Holstein
schleswig-holstein.summary: Northernmost German state bordering Denmark, historically a contested duchy whose disputed ownership between Danes and Germans sparked 19th-century wars and helped shape the German Empire.

second-schleswig-war.name: Second Schleswig War
second-schleswig-war.summary: An 1864 war in which Prussia and Austria defeated Denmark over control of Schleswig, Holstein and Lauenburg, resulting in Denmark's cession of the duchies.

german-confederation.name: German Confederation
german-confederation.summary: An association of 39 mostly German-speaking states in Central Europe from 1815 to 1866, created by the Congress of Vienna to replace the dissolved Holy Roman Empire.

north-german-confederation.name: North German Confederation
north-german-confederation.summary: State uniting northern Germany from 1867 to 1870 under Prussian leadership, formed after Prussia's victory over Austria; its states became the core of the German Empire in 1871.

veneto.name: Veneto
veneto.summary: A region in northeastern Italy, home to Venice and Verona; part of the Roman Empire, then the Republic of Venice until 1797, later Austrian territory before joining Italy in 1866.

battle-of-marengo.name: Battle of Marengo
battle-of-marengo.summary: A 14 June 1800 battle near Alessandria where Napoleon's French forces overcame a surprise Austrian attack, driving Austria from Italy and cementing his power as First Consul.

battle-of-ulm.name: Battle of Ulm
battle-of-ulm.summary: A series of skirmishes in October 1805 in which Napoleon trapped an entire Austrian army under Karl Mack near Ulm in Bavaria, forcing its surrender with minimal French losses.

treaty-of-sch-nbrunn.name: Treaty of Schönbrunn
treaty-of-sch-nbrunn.summary: 1809 treaty between France and Austria that ended the Fifth Coalition after Austria's defeat at the Battle of Wagram.

erfurt-union.name: Erfurt Union
erfurt-union.summary: A short-lived union of German states proposed by Prussia in 1850, with a parliament that met in Erfurt from March to April before the plan collapsed under Austrian pressure.

franz-joseph-i.name: Franz Joseph I
franz-joseph-i.summary: Emperor of Austria and King of Hungary who ruled the Habsburg monarchy from 1848 until his death in 1916, presiding over the creation of Austria-Hungary in 1867.

hungarian-revolution-of-1848.name: Hungarian Revolution of 1848
hungarian-revolution-of-1848.summary: A failed 1848-49 uprising against Habsburg rule that became a cornerstone of modern Hungarian national identity; its anniversary is still a national holiday.

alvensleben-convention.name: Alvensleben Convention
alvensleben-convention.summary: An 1863 treaty between the Russian Empire and the Kingdom of Prussia, signed in St. Petersburg by General Gustav von Alvensleben and Russian Foreign Minister Alexander Gorchakov.

brothers-grimm.name: Brothers Grimm
brothers-grimm.summary: German brothers, Jacob (1785-1863) and Wilhelm (1786-1859), whose 1812 folk-tale collection popularized stories like Cinderella and Snow White and shaped modern folklore studies.

struwwelpeter.name: Der Struwwelpeter
struwwelpeter.summary: An 1845 German children's book of illustrated cautionary tales by psychiatrist Heinrich Hoffmann, considered a precursor to comic books.

kurd-lasswitz.name: Kurd Lasswitz
kurd-lasswitz.summary: German author, scientist and philosopher (1848–1910), often called "the father of German science fiction".

jules-verne.name: Jules Verne
jules-verne.summary: French novelist, poet and playwright, 1828 to 1905, whose adventure novels such as Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas made him one of the most translated authors ever.

wilhelm-busch.name: Wilhelm Busch
wilhelm-busch.summary: German humorist, poet and illustrator (1832–1908) whose innovative illustrated tales, including Max and Moritz, deeply influenced later comic artists.

max-and-moritz.name: Max and Moritz
max-and-moritz.summary: An 1865 German illustrated verse story by Wilhelm Busch about seven boyish pranks, which had wide cultural influence and inspired later comic strips.

two-planets.name: Auf zwei Planeten (Two Planets)
two-planets.summary: 1897 German science fiction novel by Kurd Lasswitz imagining intelligent life on Mars, exploring colonization and the clash of civilizations.

the-tunnel-kellermann-novel.name: Der Tunnel
the-tunnel-kellermann-novel.summary: Bernhard Kellermann's 1913 novel about social progress and modern technology, which sold 100,000 copies within six months and became one of the era's biggest bestsellers, reaching millions of copies by 1939.

deutsches-w-rterbuch.name: Deutsches Wörterbuch
deutsches-w-rterbuch.summary: The largest, most comprehensive dictionary of the German language, begun by the Brothers Grimm in 1838 and finally completed by later scholars in 1961.

carl-grunert.name: Carl Grunert
carl-grunert.summary: German poet and writer (1865–1918) known for stories, plays and poems, and an avid reader interested in Kurd Laßwitz's work.

neo-kantianism.name: Neo-Kantianism
neo-kantianism.summary: A late modern revival of Immanuel Kant's 18th-century philosophy that sought to develop and clarify his ideas, particularly the thing-in-itself and his moral philosophy.

gustav-fechner.name: Gustav Fechner
gustav-fechner.summary: A German physicist, philosopher and experimental psychologist (1801–1887) who founded psychophysics and showed a mathematical relationship between physical stimuli and sensation.

h-g-wells.name: H. G. Wells
h-g-wells.summary: English writer (1866–1946) of more than forty novels, often called the 'father of science fiction' for works like The Time Machine that imagined time travel and alien invasion.

otto-von-bismarck.name: Otto von Bismarck
otto-von-bismarck.summary: German statesman (1815–1898) who oversaw the unification of Germany through three wars and served as its first chancellor from 1871 to 1890, known as the "Iron Chancellor."

wilhelm-r-ntgen.name: Wilhelm Röntgen
wilhelm-r-ntgen.summary: German physicist (1845–1923) who discovered X-rays and became the first recipient of the Nobel Prize in Physics, in 1901.

roentgenium.name: Roentgenium
roentgenium.summary: Extremely radioactive synthetic chemical element (symbol Rg, atomic number 111), first created in 1994 and named after the physicist who discovered X-rays.

heinrich-hertz.name: Heinrich Hertz
heinrich-hertz.summary: German physicist (1857–1894) who first conclusively proved the existence of the electromagnetic waves predicted by Maxwell's equations.

joseph-von-fraunhofer.name: Joseph von Fraunhofer
joseph-von-fraunhofer.summary: German physicist and optical lens maker (1787–1826) who invented the spectroscope and discovered the dark absorption lines in the sun's spectrum now called Fraunhofer lines.

fraunhofer-lines.name: Fraunhofer lines
fraunhofer-lines.summary: Dark absorption lines in the Sun's optical spectrum, formed when atoms in its atmosphere absorb light from below; named for German physicist Joseph von Fraunhofer, who observed them in 1814.

hermann-von-helmholtz.name: Hermann von Helmholtz
hermann-von-helmholtz.summary: German physicist and physician (1821–1894) known for foundational work on the conservation of energy, thermodynamics, and the physiology of vision and hearing.

albert-einstein.name: Albert Einstein
albert-einstein.summary: German-born theoretical physicist (1879–1955) who developed the theory of relativity and won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics.

max-planck.name: Max Planck
max-planck.summary: German theoretical physicist (1858–1947) who originated quantum theory, is known for the Planck constant, and won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics.

perrotine-printing.name: Louis-Jérôme Perrot
perrotine-printing.summary: A French inventor (1798–1878) who created the perrotine, a mechanical block-printing machine that remained widely used in France, Germany and Italy.

house-of-habsburg-lorraine.name: Habsburg-Lorraine
house-of-habsburg-lorraine.summary: The line formed after the 1736 marriage of Francis III of Lorraine and Maria Theresa of Austria, uniting the Habsburg and Lorraine houses in later Austrian rulers.

wilhelm-i.name: Wilhelm I
wilhelm-i.summary: King of Prussia from 1861 and the first German Emperor, from 1871 until his death in 1888, as head of the newly united Germany.

house-of-hohenzollern.name: Hohenzollern dynasty
house-of-hohenzollern.summary: A German dynasty originating in Swabia around 1061 that ruled Brandenburg, Prussia and, from 1871, the German Empire, until its overthrow in 1918.

kulturkampf.name: Kulturkampf
kulturkampf.summary: Seven-year political conflict (1871–1878) between the Catholic Church in Germany and the Kingdom of Prussia under Chancellor Bismarck over control of education and church appointments, marked also by anti-Polish sentiment.

dual-alliance-1879.name: Dual Alliance
dual-alliance-1879.summary: A defensive treaty signed by Germany and Austria-Hungary in 1879 promising mutual support against a Russian attack, part of Bismarck's strategy to avoid German isolation.

triple-alliance-1882.name: Triple Alliance (1882)
triple-alliance-1882.summary: A defensive alliance formed in 1882 between Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy, renewed periodically until 1915, though Italy ultimately fought World War I on the Allied side.

austro-hungarian-compromise-of-1867.name: Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867
austro-hungarian-compromise-of-1867.summary: The 1867 agreement that created the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary, restoring Hungary's separate constitution and status after Emperor Franz Joseph's post-1848 absolutist rule.

battle-of-austerlitz.name: Battle of Austerlitz
battle-of-austerlitz.summary: The decisive 2 December 1805 battle of the War of the Third Coalition, in which Napoleon's Grande Armée defeated a combined Russian and Austrian army led by Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II.

confederation-of-the-rhine.name: Confederation of the Rhine
confederation-of-the-rhine.summary: A confederation of German client states set up by Napoleon after defeating Austria and Russia at Austerlitz, lasting from 1806 to 1813 and prompting the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire.

prince-elector.name: Prince-elector
prince-elector.summary: A member of the Electoral College of the Holy Roman Empire who elected the Holy Roman Emperor, a privileged office that existed until the empire's dissolution in 1806.

kingdom-of-w-rttemberg.name: Kingdom of Württemberg
kingdom-of-w-rttemberg.summary: A German state from 1806 to 1918 in what is now Baden-Württemberg, created when Napoleon elevated the Electorate of Württemberg to a kingdom under Frederick I.

baden.name: Baden
baden.summary: A historical territory in southern Germany, once spanning both banks of the Upper Rhine but confined to the eastern side since the Napoleonic Wars.

landgraviate-of-hesse-kassel.name: Hesse-Kassel
landgraviate-of-hesse-kassel.summary: A state of the Holy Roman Empire created in 1567 and ruled from Kassel, elevated to an Electorate in 1803 under Napoleon's reorganization of the empire.

w-rttemberg.name: Württemberg
w-rttemberg.summary: Historical German territory in the Swabia region centered on Stuttgart, now part of the state of Baden-Württemberg.

salzburg-state.name: Salzburg
salzburg-state.summary: An Austrian state bordering Germany and Italy, historically tied to the Prince-Archbishopric of Salzburg, an ecclesiastical territory of the Holy Roman Empire that was secularized in 1803.

kingdom-of-westphalia.name: Kingdom of Westphalia
kingdom-of-westphalia.summary: A French client state in present-day Germany from 1807 to 1813, ruled by Napoleon's brother Jérôme Bonaparte, that introduced Germany's first written modern constitution and equal rights for Jews.

regensburg.name: Regensburg
regensburg.summary: A city in eastern Bavaria at the confluence of the Danube, Naab and Regen rivers, founded as a Roman river fort and later home to the Holy Roman Empire's Perpetual Diet.

w-rzburg.name: Würzburg
w-rzburg.summary: City in northern Bavaria, Germany, on the Main river, known for its historic old town and the Würzburger Residenz, a UNESCO World Heritage palace.

frederick-iii-german-emperor.name: Frederick III, German Emperor
frederick-iii-german-emperor.summary: German Emperor and King of Prussia for just 99 days in 1888, a liberal-minded crown prince married to Queen Victoria's daughter, who died of throat cancer soon after taking the throne.

frederick-the-great.name: Frederick the Great
frederick-the-great.summary: King of Prussia from 1740 to 1786 who annexed Silesia, made Prussia a major European power, reorganized its army, and patronized the Enlightenment as an enlightened absolutist ruler.

helmuth-von-moltke-the-younger.name: Helmuth von Moltke the Younger
helmuth-von-moltke-the-younger.summary: A German general and Chief of the German General Staff from 1906, who led the army as commander-in-chief in the early months of World War I; his role in 1914 remains controversial.

gordon-a-craig.name: Gordon A. Craig
gordon-a-craig.summary: Scottish-American historian (1913–2005) known for his work on German history and diplomatic history.

july-crisis.name: July Crisis
july-crisis.summary: The chain of diplomatic and military escalations among European powers in mid-1914, beginning with the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, that led to the outbreak of World War I.

immanuel-kant.name: Immanuel Kant
immanuel-kant.summary: German Enlightenment philosopher (1724–1804) whose work on knowledge, ethics and metaphysics, especially the Critique of Pure Reason, made him among the most influential thinkers in Western philosophy.

johann-gottlieb-fichte.name: Fichte
johann-gottlieb-fichte.summary: German philosopher (1762–1814) and founding figure of German idealism, known for his work on self-consciousness; the thesis–antithesis–synthesis idea, often credited to Hegel, actually originated with him.

friedrich-wilhelm-joseph-schelling.name: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling
friedrich-wilhelm-joseph-schelling.summary: A German philosopher seen as a bridge between Fichte and Hegel in the development of German idealism, whose evolving philosophy is considered difficult to interpret.

georg-wilhelm-friedrich-hegel.name: Hegel
georg-wilhelm-friedrich-hegel.summary: German philosopher (1770–1831) and major figure in German idealism, whose dialectical system, 'absolute idealism,' shaped modern metaphysics, political philosophy and philosophy of religion.

german-idealism.name: German idealism
german-idealism.summary: A philosophical movement in Germany in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, developed from Kant's work and including Fichte, Schelling and Hegel.

materialism-controversy.name: Materialism controversy
materialism-controversy.summary: A mid-19th-century German public debate over whether new scientific findings, especially in biology, were compatible with belief in the soul, God, and free will.

carl-vogt.name: Carl Vogt
carl-vogt.summary: A German scientist, philosopher and politician (1817–1895) who emigrated to Switzerland, publishing notable works on zoology, geology and physiology while active in politics, including the 1848–49 Frankfurt Parliament.

ernst-mach.name: Ernst Mach
ernst-mach.summary: Austrian physicist and philosopher (1838–1916) who studied shock waves, gave his name to the Mach number, and whose critique of Newton foreshadowed Einstein's relativity.

neutral-monism.name: Neutral Monism
neutral-monism.summary: A philosophical theory holding that reality is fundamentally neither mental nor physical, proposed as a possible answer to the mind-body problem.

joseph-dietzgen.name: Joseph Dietzgen
joseph-dietzgen.summary: German socialist philosopher and journalist credited with independently developing the theory of dialectical materialism associated with Marx and Engels.

karl-marx.name: Karl Marx
karl-marx.summary: German philosopher and revolutionary socialist (1818-1883) who developed historical materialism and co-authored The Communist Manifesto with Friedrich Engels; his ideas, Marxism, greatly influenced political and social history.

friedrich-engels.name: Friedrich Engels
friedrich-engels.summary: A German philosopher and revolutionary socialist who co-wrote The Communist Manifesto with Karl Marx and completed Marx's Das Kapital after his death.

wilhelm-dilthey.name: Wilhelm Dilthey
wilhelm-dilthey.summary: German philosopher (1833–1911) who held Hegel's former chair at the University of Berlin and worked to establish the methodological foundations of history and the human sciences.

friedrich-nietzsche.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
friedrich-nietzsche.summary: A German philosopher and former classical philologist known for critiquing objective truth and Christian morality, who suffered a mental collapse in 1889.

georg-simmel.name: Georg Simmel
georg-simmel.summary: German sociologist, philosopher and critic (1858–1918) and a founding figure of sociology, known for pioneering analyses of individuality, social fragmentation and urban life.

ludwig-klages.name: Ludwig Klages
ludwig-klages.summary: German philosopher, psychologist and graphologist (1872–1956), twice nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature, central to the Lebensphilosophie school of thought.

lebensphilosophie.name: Lebensphilosophie
lebensphilosophie.summary: A German philosophical movement of the late 19th and early 20th centuries emphasizing life's meaning and value, drawing on Schopenhauer and Nietzsche and influencing later existentialism.

ludwig-b-chner.name: Ludwig Büchner
ludwig-b-chner.summary: German philosopher, physiologist and physician (1824–1899) and a leading exponent of 19th-century scientific materialism.

rudolf-wagner.name: Rudolf Wagner
rudolf-wagner.summary: A German anatomist and physiologist (1805–1864), co-discoverer of the germinal vesicle, known for research on ganglia, nerve endings and the sympathetic nerves.

justus-von-liebig.name: Justus von Liebig
justus-von-liebig.summary: German chemist (1803–1873) considered a founder of organic chemistry, called the "father of the fertilizer industry" for showing nitrogen and minerals are essential plant nutrients.

gustav-kirchhoff.name: Gustav Kirchhoff
gustav-kirchhoff.summary: A German physicist and mathematician (1824–1887) who contributed to the understanding of electrical circuits, spectroscopy and black-body radiation, and coined the term 'black body.'

ludwig-boltzmann.name: Ludwig Boltzmann
ludwig-boltzmann.summary: Austrian physicist (1844–1906) who developed statistical mechanics and gave the modern definition of entropy, later honored by the naming of the Boltzmann constant.

boltzmann-brain.name: Boltzmann brain
boltzmann-brain.summary: A thought experiment holding that a brain with false memories is statistically more likely to spontaneously form than the entire universe is to arise as cosmologists describe.

ernst-kapp.name: Ernst Kapp
ernst-kapp.summary: German-American philosopher of technology and geographer (1808–1896) who fled Germany after a sedition prosecution and settled in Texas, working as a farmer and inventor.

marshall-mcluhan.name: Marshall McLuhan
marshall-mcluhan.summary: Canadian philosopher (1911–1980) known as the father of media studies, who coined the phrase "the medium is the message" and the term "global village".

centre-party-germany.name: Centre Party (Germany)
centre-party-germany.summary: A German Catholic political party founded in 1870 that resisted Bismarck's Kulturkampf, became a major force under the Weimar Republic, and dissolved itself in 1933 under Nazi pressure.

reichstag-german-empire.name: Reichstag
reichstag-german-empire.summary: Germany's parliament from 1871 to 1918, sharing legislative power with the Bundesrat though the emperor held little political power over it.

turners.name: Turners
turners.summary: Members of German-American gymnastic clubs called Turnvereine, who promoted German culture and liberal politics and helped establish gymnastics as an American sport and academic subject.

german-freethinkers-league.name: German Freethinkers League
german-freethinkers-league.summary: An organization founded by German freethinkers and atheists to oppose the power of state churches, banned by the Nazis in 1933 and later reestablished in West Germany.
